abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>
<jats:list>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>Plants adjust their size and reproductive effort in response to numerous selection pressures and constraints. The self‐thinning law describes a well‐known trade‐off between size and density. Plants also trade‐off investment into growth vs. sexual reproduction, as described by life‐history theory.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>We build on past work on plant allometry and life history by examining both self‐thinning and size‐dependent reproduction in a single plant species, the saltmarsh grass <jats:italic>Spartina alterniflora</jats:italic>, across a wide range of settings: three landscape positions, two habitats and eight sites, across sixteen years.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>Plants in different landscape positions and years varied tremendously in size and shoot density. However, all this variation could be explained by a single allometric relationship consistent with the self‐thinning law, but with a lower slope. Flowering was size‐dependent, and the size at which plants had a 50% probability of flowering varied among habitat, sites and years. Plants that were stressed reproduced at a smaller size than plants that were growing under good conditions, and this pattern was consistent among habitat, sites and years. Finally, reproductive biomass and the proportion of shoots flowering increased with increasing vegetative size (plant height or shoot biomass). Combining these two patterns, <jats:italic>S. alterniflora</jats:italic> plants growing high density are small and reproduce at a smaller size than large plants growing at low density.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>Although there is tremendous spatial and temporal variation in <jats:italic>S. alterniflora</jats:italic> growth and reproductive patterns, all this variation can be understood as resulting from two simple allometric trade‐offs. Because saltmarsh plants often occur in monospecific stands, they may serve as simple, model systems for studies of plant life history.</jats:p></jats:list-item>
</jats:list>
</jats:p><jats:p>A free <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2435.13384/suppinfo">Plain Language Summary</jats:ext-link> can be found within the Supporting Information of this article.</jats:p>
title: Self‐thinning and size‐dependent flowering of the grass Spartina alterniflora across space and time
